Friary
FRY-uh-ree
n. (a convent of friars; a mendicant house, usually set in a town rather than in the wilderness)
From friar, Old French frere, Latin frater, a brother; with the place-suffix -y. The brothers' house.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A friary is a house of friars, and its siting tells the whole story of the mendicant movement. The old monasteries were planted in valleys and on moors, deliberately away from men; the friaries were built in towns, in the poorest quarters, next to the markets and the schools. The friars came to preach, and preaching requires hearers: “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14), and “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15). In that the friars recovered something the cloister had lost. A friary was not self-sufficient, held little land, and depended on the town it served, which kept it close to ordinary people and gave the orders their early popularity. The defects followed from the same closeness. Friaries competed with parish clergy for burials, confessions and legacies; their preachers were often licensed over the heads of local pastors; and houses vowed to poverty accumulated handsome buildings by gift. Chaucer's friar is not a Protestant slander but a medieval complaint. Still, the impulse that built them — take the word to where the people are — is one Scripture plainly commends.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines friary as a monastery or convent of friars, and as an adjective like a friar; friar as an appellation given to monks who live in convents; and convent as a house for persons devoted to religion, an abbey or monastery.

expand to see more

FRIARY, n. A monastery; a convent of friars.

FRIARY, a. Like a friar; pertaining to friars or to a monastery.

FRIAR, n. An appellation common to the monks of all orders; those who live in convents or houses of religious retirement.

CONVENT, n. A house for persons devoted to religion; an abbey; a monastery; a nunnery.

PREACH, v.i. To pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject, or from a text of scripture.

Key Scripture

Rom 10:14 — "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?"

Mar 16:15 — "And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature."

Rom 10:15 — "And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!"

2Ti 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

Modern Corruption

A town convent of friars: the gospel carried to where people actually live, in houses that were vowed to poverty and grew rich by legacy.

expand to see more

The real corruption of the friaries was institutional hypocrisy, and it was named at the time. Houses sworn to own nothing came to hold fine churches, libraries and rents, received by gift so that the vow might technically stand. Paul's warning about ministry for gain fits exactly: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith” (1Ti 6:10). A vow kept by a legal fiction is worse than no vow, because it teaches the conscience to reason in fictions.

The principle to recover is the siting, not the vow. The friars were right that the gospel must be preached where men are, and right that a preacher tied to the rich will flatter them. “How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace” (Rom 10:15) commends the going; nothing in Scripture commends the pretence of destitution that later came with it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin frater, a brother; Greek adelphos (G80), a brother; Greek kerusso (G2784), to proclaim as a herald; Greek euaggelizo (G2097), to bring good news; Hebrew basar (H1319), to bear tidings.

expand to see more

Latin frater — a brother; the friar is a brother rather than a father, which was the point of the name.

Greek adelphos (G80) — brother; “one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8).

Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim as a herald; “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).

Greek euaggelizo (G2097) — to announce good news; the verb behind “evangelise”.

Hebrew basar (H1319) — to bear tidings; “the feet of him that bringeth good tidings” (Isa 52:7).

Usage

"“Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15) — the commission the friaries were built to serve."

"“how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) — the argument for a house in the town rather than the moor."

"“For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10) — the reef the friaries struck."
